Dear Terrence,

Many thanks for your responses to my questions. The polyserial correlation warning crops up between my outcome variable which is continuous and some of the items that are making up my latent variables (these are either binary or ordered factor items). I ran polyserial correlations using the polycor package and this gave me correlations between my outcome and each item. I am unsure why the polyserial correlation is unable to converge between my continuous outcome and the items using the lavaan package. Do you have any ideas what my causing this problem and/or any solutions?

Many thanks
Kirsty

Try to exclude some items with loadings below of 0.5 or 0.6. Be careful don't affect the sense and kernel of construct factor.
Get the modification indices of your cfa model with this command: `lavaan::modindices(fit,  sort. = TRUE, maximum.number = 20)` . This output allow you see cross-loadings on items or suggestions of correlations between error variance.

messages.subject: 2-1-1 SEM model with continuous outcomes and binary predictor
messages.subject_clean: 2-1-1 SEM model with continuous outcomes and binary predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm doing a SEM model in a longitudinal study (n = 271) with a binary IV at level 2 and various continuous predictors at level 1 (cluster in 22 classrooms).

However, I repeatedly got this error:

Error in lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan ERROR
    Some between-level (only) variables have non-zero variance at the
    within-level. Please double-check your data.

De plus : Warning messages:
1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Level-1 variable “T2EMOPOSIT” has no variance within some
    clusters. The cluster ids with zero within variance are: 303
2: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Level-2 variable “COND” has non-zero variance at the within level.
    The cluster ids with non-zero within variance are: 707A 304

Thank you very much for your help!

Jordane

Any scaling method is arbitrary, including the "non-arbitrary" effects-coding method.  Here is an informative article on the topic:

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1517356

The lavaan forum is for questions about the software.  General SEM questions can be posted on SEMNET:

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1

But if you are interested in the effects-coding method, lavaan has implemented it.  See the effect.coding description on the ?lavOptions help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

First, please include your lavaan() call.

Warning 1: What are the raw-data scales for WP and PRE?

Having observed variables with widely varying metrics can cause
computational problems. Look at descriptive statistics for your
observed variables. If the variances of some of the variables are much
larger (lavaan says >1000x) than the variances of the others. One
possibility to check is if you have some numeric missing value flags
(e.g., 999 on a 1-5 scale).

If the values are correct, the usual practice is to divide the values
of the large one by a constant to bring the variances in line. This
will not affect statistical conclusions from the model, though you may
need to go back and rescale the unstandardized parameter estimates
afterward if the resulting scaling is not intuitive.

Fixing this can sometimes help with the NPD error, so I'd try it first.

As for Warning 2, it is what it says it is. You've got an N of 16,
possibly in just one group (again, you haven't sent the lavaan call).
What missing data method did you specify? If you didn't specify, I
think the default is listwise deletion, so you've lost most of your
sample.

Pat

This message from your original post suggests it was included in your Level-1 model.  Do you still get this warning with the syntax you posted?  Because it would indeed be strange if lavaan were complaining about this being a within-level variable when it does not appear in your within-level model.

>   lavaan WARNING:
>     Level-1 variable “T2EMOPOSIT” has no variance within some
>     clusters. The cluster ids with zero within variance are: 303

This message is pretty informative.  It is also only a warning (in case there might be a problem), not an error.  If your error message went away after excluding COND from the within-level model, then you should still be able to view your results.  Using lavaan's example data, you can see there is no actual problem (though a warning) when you set all values of x1 within a single cluster to the same value:

data(Demo.twolevel)
Demo.twolevel$x1[Demo.twolevel$cluster == 1L] <- 0
model <- '
    level: 1
        fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3
        fw ~ x1 + x2 + x3
    level: 2
        fb =~ y1 + y2 + y3
        fb ~ w1 + w2
'
fit <- sem(model, data = Demo.twolevel, cluster = "cluster")

messages.subject: Re: any prediction option for lavaan.mi with categorical data?
messages.subject_clean: any prediction option for lavaan.mi with categorical data?
messages.body_plain:
> ...even a qualified "no" would actually help...in some way...

You have correctly identified the limits of the software.  lavaan has a predict() method for lavaan objects, but semTools does not have a predict() method for lavaan.mi objects.  Because of the inherent limitations of using factor-score estimates as known values in subsequent analyses, I have not been motivated to develop a predict() method for lavaan.mi objects, but I did provide plausibleValues().  However, lavaan does not provide the SEs or asymptotic covariance matrix of factor score estimates for the methods available for categorical indicators; thus, there is no mechanism for plausibleValues() to do its job in that context.

Mplus would be able to provide plausible values for categorical indicators themselves (LRESPONSES), as well as for factor scores, using Bayesian estimation with categorical indicators:  https://www.statmodel.com/download/Plausible.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Ok. If the N really is 16, that is your problem, and it's what lavaan
is telling you is the problem.

Your larger model is almost certainly empirically underidentified.
It's not specific to lavaan. That's probably also why you have the NPD
error.

For some of your other questions:

"Is it ok if one variable is divided by 10 and another by 1000 for example?"

Yes. Linear transformations such as addition and division by a
constant do not affect the substantive results, but can make
computations easier.

Order of variables does not matter.

mod1 <-

'

fit <- cfa.mi(mod1, data = dat_imputed, estimator = 'WLSMV', ordered = c('ind1', 'ind2', 'ind3'))
summary(fit)

messages.subject_clean: Parallel growth model
messages.body_plain:
Everything Pat said is correct. One word of caution is using multiple imputation with 16 people... I would strongly suggest using mice to make 10-20 data sets and then pool your estimates. So the `semTools` package will be needed. You'll call growth.mi() to a mice object (that has not had mice::complete() called to it (i.e., the m = 20 data sets)).

Anyways, I wanted to offer 3 more avenues to explore (assuming I interpret your message correctly). I am offering this because I sadly think 16 will be too small to answer your desired question.

As a note: I am a doctoral student in a quantitative research methods PhD, but again, I'm still a student and maybe a long-time expert can suggest something I didn't think of or shoot one of these ideas down.

> 1) If you have 850,000 data points which are all measured at 4 time points in 16 people, you could explore nested models which treat the 16 people as "groups" with times nested inside that, and then you'd actually have 850,000 data points at 4 times which is way more than you'd need for this. But to be fully honest, I don't know if lavaan can handle 3 levels of nesting... You might have to go to an HLM-type software or Mplus. Admittedly, I did not follow you perfectly when you explained this (because I'm a social scientist) so I'm not sure if this will work for you.

> 2) You could try a data reduction method. Maybe consider latent classes of these constructs (within individuals), so that you are looking at growth of fewer constructs. And although you won't have every construct mapped, you'll have a gist of how "groups" of constructs move.

> 3) The most fool-proof way--but also a way publications may push against--is to simply plot these in ggplot. You could do this two ways:
> > a) get the individual growth curves, ask lavaan for the parameter estimates, and get each construct's intercept and slope for each participant. You'd then take the average slope (& the standard error) across people and plot these. If SEs don't overlap, you have a rough estimate of significance.
> > b) do the same thing without lavaan (i.e., plot the constructs over time) and fit a linear model to it and see if SEs overlap.

Method 1 will likely give you a headache with implementing in and interpreting from software.
Method 2 will be very hard to concretely conceptualize and explain to others you did it "right" (conceptually, I mean, not in the software).
Method 3 does not take into account other constructs so you're essentially assuming they're fully independent by using different models, and if it's biology things are rarely fully independent. But people tend to like visuals so maybe it'll be sufficient for your purposes.

As an aside, SEM (and all of frequentist statistics) is not so good with data sets where the number of variables is larger than the number of participants. If you wanted to predict something, machine learning methods like random forests or decision trees can do that, but again those are less valid for inference than prediction (and few people have implemented these in interesting longitudinal ways like you're looking for).

Good luck!

messages.subject_clean: Clarification on which coefficients of CFA with ordered indicators are probit
messages.body_plain:
> Which part of this model will use probit coefficients, just the loadings of the manifest onto their latent factor?

Yes, any outcome that is discrete will be linked to its predictors via a probit function.

> The regression from the covariates to the latent variable will not be a probit coefficient, correct?

There are many latent variables in your model (e.g., one latent item-response per dichotomous outcome).  The common factor is assumed normally distributed so it is linked to predictors via the identity function (i.e., regular linear effects as you would find in OLS regression).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: LGM baseline estimation failed?
messages.subject_clean: LGM baseline estimation failed?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
we are fitting a substantial lgm (12 waves, N=25k). Model estimation proceeds normally, fit stats (e.g. chi sq=630, df=63, rmsea=0.022) and parameters look sensible. However, lavaan reports that the 'baseline model estimation has failed'. This is a bit inconvenient as it doesn't allow us to compute e.g. CFI to report. I have tried the same model in e.g. Onyx to see whether it was our data/model but I could reproduce the fit/parameter estimates exactly for the hypothesized model, and the baseline model converged fine ion onyx. One might be inclined to switch to onyx but that is slow to estimate for large models and cumbersome for multigroup models (despite its many other strengths), so I'd rather stick with lavaan. I also reproduced the same model in openmx which also computed a nullmodel just fine, but openmyx seems very sensitive to starting values and MLR/multigroup constraints (and general syntax) are much more inconvenient, so again I prefer lavaan if at all possible - Do you have any suggestions for us, or further information to share? Should we go back a few lavaan versions perhaps?

messages.subject: Re: Difference on regression coefficients in lavaan vs Mplus and PROCESS - path analysis
messages.subject_clean: Difference on regression coefficients in lavaan vs Mplus and PROCESS - path analysis
messages.body_plain:
There is a difference in syntax. The Mplus code says:

INCL with EXCL;

but the lavaan syntax says:

 INCL ~ EXCL

Mplus allows for residual covariance , but lavaan is told to make EXCL a predictor of INCL, along with the other predictors--oddly, lavaan presents results for this last predictor of INCL differently.

Try changing the lavaan line to use ~~ (covariance) instead of ~ (regression), or change the Mplus syntax.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to run a Wald test. Essentially I have a Heywood case for one of my latent variables where the variance for the latent is negative, but none of the individual indicators are negative.

My model is below:

#install.packages("lavaan") #for SEM
library(lavaan)

mymodel <- '

#measurement model

ent =~ sdes_q1 + sdes_q4 +  sdes_q6 + sdes_q8

def =~ sdes_q2 + sdes_q3 + sdes_q5 + sdes_q7

idea =~ dssis_q1r + dssis_q2r + dssis_q3r + dssis_q4r

dep =~ cessds_q1 + cessds_q2 + cessds_q3 + cessds_q4 + cessds_q5r + cessds_q6 + cessds_q7 + cessds_q8r + cessds_q9 + cessds_q10

#structural model

def ~ dep

ent ~ def + dep

idea ~  ent + dep'

# model identification and estimation
modelfit <- sem(mymodel, data = mydatat1, estimator = "MLM")

summary(modelfit_ideation, fit.measures = T, standardized = T, rsquare = T)

The result gives me a negative error variance for ent only  (-0.011).

I can confirm too that there are no outliers on this variable (the distribution is actually somewhat bimodal with floor/ceiling effects).

I've done some reading around Heywood cases, and I've seen that a Wald test can explore this further. I've run:

lavTestWald(mymodel, "ent")

But this gives me an error: Error in lavParseModelString(constraints) : lavaan ERROR: model does not contain lavaan syntax (no operators found)

I'm otherwise pretty stuck - I've tried more simply YouTube videos etc, but there aren't any on how to handle Heywood cases specifically in R.

Any help is really appreciated.

Rosie

messages.subject: Re: Wald test
messages.subject_clean: Wald test
messages.body_plain:
> I have a Heywood case

You can print the 95% CI instead:

summary(fit, ci = TRUE)

Then just check that the CI includes positive values (in which case you can't reject the H0 that the true residual variance > 0)

> lavTestWald(mymodel, "ent")

You are not specifying a constraint to be tested.  If you label the parameter in the model syntax, then you can specify a constraint that this parameter == 0 (or a small, positive number, but again the CI is easier because it is the entire range of H0 values that cannot be rejected by the data).  See the help-page for examples.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

Hello all,

I'm trying to run a CFA with ordinal and binary indicators. When I run the following code...

I get the same message when I estimate with WLSMV, or change missing to using "listwise", "pairwise", or "available.cases".

I have tried running the model with and without manifest covariances that could account for some potential autocorrelation between variables, without any change.

I have tried running with both Lavaan 0.6-6 and the current dev version, without any change.

I have tried both theta and delta parameterization, as well as not specifying the parameterization.

I cannot find any explanation of what "NA/NaN Hessian evaluation" means, and I am having trouble understanding the rest of the error message.

Any ideas?

Good morning,

I am writing syntax to produce a growth model. The models work fine, but the diagrams are a mess. The syntax for my diagram, and an example diagram, are attached:

semPaths(se.fit, what='est', edge.color = "black", fade = FALSE, layout = "tree2")
title("SE LGM", line=1)

I was wondering if anyone could make any suggestions to make this more aesthetically pleasing? In particular I'm trying to stop the path widths being determined by their coefficient (e.g. that chunky dashed line on the right), and stop any coefficients overlapping each other. Any suggestions on how to rectify these/generally make the diagram better would be much appreciated.

Regards,

Dave

messages.body_plain:
It can be done with lavaan with "phantom variables."

Grimm & Ram have syntax for doing it in Mplus in Appendix A here:
https://www.statmodel.com/download/SEM-Grimm2009.pdf (though of course
you should read the whole article for context). They don't use
anything lavaan can't do.

Pat

messages.subject: New warning in lavaan 0.6-6: "estimation pearson correlation did not converge for..."
messages.subject_clean: New warning in lavaan 0.6-6: "estimation pearson correlation did not converge for..."
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been fitting cfa and sem models using lavaan for a few weeks, but having updated to the latest version today I am now getting a warning on models that previously converged OK. Can someone tell me what this means and how to correct it please?

The warning  - repeated for up to 5 pairs of variables, within and across different latent factors - is:

lav_bvreg_cor_twostep_fit(fit.y1 = UNI[[i]], fit.y2 = UNI[[j]],  :   lavaan WARNING: estimation pearson correlation did not converge for variables ...[ names of two indicator variables ]

I've checked the residual correlations and these are a) present and b) OK (<0.1). What else should I look for?

As a background, this is fitted to a data set of approx 1000 observations; three of the indicator variables (all on the same latent variable) are treated as ordinal but the assumption of multivariate normality is violated in most of the continuous variables anyway. I am using the default DWLS  estimator with robust se's. Fit is thus far not satisfactory as far as model chi-squared is concerned - hence still playing with these models - but other fit measures were adequate (TLI, CFI, NFI all >0.95, RMSEA ~0.04). An example is below, though I'm getting these warnings for every model I'd previously fitted:

mod <- "
              S1 =~ ind1+ ind2
              S2 =~ ind3 + ind4 + ind5 + ind6
              S3 =~ ind7 + ind8 + ind9
              "
fit <- cfa(mod, std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE<, data=basedf, ordered=c("ind7","ind8","ind9"), missing="pairwise")

This is my first post on a forum ever - hope someone can help!

Many thanks,

Rebecca

I believe that this uses a polychoric correlation matrix by default as soon as the "ordered=" argument is specified in the call to cfa and sem (or even if it isn't, if the variables are already declared as ordered in the dataset). At least, the models do  estimate thresholds and intercepts which they would not for straightforward ML procedures. Do you think this is the reason for the warning?

Best wishes,

Rebecca

Can anybody clarify why it is now appearing? I can just revert to the old version of lavaan but if it's telling me something about my model/data/misspecification then I'd prefer to know!

Thank you for your suggestions so far.

Rebecca

messages.subject: Bivariate Parallel Process Modelling; Continuous and Ordinal variables
messages.subject_clean: Bivariate Parallel Process Modelling; Continuous and Ordinal variables
messages.body_plain:
Respected members, experts and colleagues,

I am looking forward to investigate the dynamics of two concepts repeatedly measured over time. Following are the considerations in that regard.

1. The first concept (say, economic_outcome) is measured by a continous indicator [basically, we have 12 months dataset, and economic_outcome is measured as "income", a continuous variable at each of the months)

2. The second concept is a bit complicated. First the concept is composed of three sub-components, each with ordinal indicators.

For example (only for demonstrative purpose; not the real set of variables):
The second concept is say, students_cog_ability, with three sub-concepts each measured in 3-level ordinal scale; data collected in each of the 12 months.

 a. attentiveness (0- bad, 1 - average, 2 - good), b. responsiveness (0- bad, 1 - average, 2 - good) , c. expressiveness (0- bad, 1 - average, 2 - good)

There are no missing data.

My research objectives are the following:

(only for example, not the real research question).
a. Investigate the dynamics of economic outcome and student's cognitive ability
- how do the growth process of economic outcome and student's cognitive ability relate to each other.

My model

I intend to formulate a parallel process modelling.
I would like to estimate the means, variances, and covariances of intercept and slopes of the parallel latent growth trajectories of economic outcome and students_cog_ability (and/or the sub-components of students cog ability)

I believe that for the second concept (students_cog_ability) and subsequent sub-concepts, I need to construct the 'latent growth curve modelling with polytomous outcome', as also detailed in (Grimm, Ram, & Estabrook, 2017, p. 335)

I am also following the online resources by PennState Social Science Research Institute, who have remarkably preseted lavaan codes to implement models discussed in the book by Grimm, Ram, & Estabrook (2017). The 'latent growth curve modelling with polytomous outcome' model is discussed in Chapter 13 of the book, and the lavaan codes can be found in the mentioned online resource at https://quantdev.ssri.psu.edu/sites/qdev/files/GM_Chp13_tutorial.html.
However, due to the nature of the data used for the demonstration, we cannot really see the lavaan results.

My questions

I would like to seek your expert guidance on the following methodological conundrums that I'm facing.

a. Do you think it is possible to construct a parallel process model with two concepts measured differently (one is measured as a continuous manifest variable;  the other as an ordinal manifest variable), considering my research question?

b. Is it possible to combine attentiveness, responsiveness, and expressiveness into one single concept student_cog_ability; and investigate the parallel process of economic outcome and student_cog_ability?

or, should I do it separately, for example: i. parallel process of economic_outcome and responsiveness, ii. parallel process of economic_outcome and attentiveness, iii. parallel process of economic_outcome and expressiveness?

c. In the tutorial https://quantdev.ssri.psu.edu/sites/qdev/files/GM_Chp13_tutorial.html, the author has included start() function, and provided a starting value. Could you please explain what does this function really do, and how can we determine which specific starting values should we set?

I look forward to your guidance.

Thank you.

Gopal Trital
Research Scholar
University of Pavia, Italy

Reference

Allison Gray, M. S. (2020): Tutorials | Quantdev. Available online at https://quantdev.ssri.psu.edu/tutorials, updated on 7/15/2020, checked on 7/15/2020.

Grimm, K. J., Ram, N., & Estabrook, R. (2017). Growth modeling: Structural equation and multilevel modeling approaches. Methodology in the social sciences. New York NY: Guilford Press.

messages.subject: Question on testing multi-sample Structural Equation Modeling using lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Question on testing multi-sample Structural Equation Modeling using lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I use lavaan to conduct multi-sample Structural Equation Modeling. In the analysis, I examine whether the pattern of mediation would differ by two (categorical) groups with the use of following scripts:

mediation.model <-
  '
# Measurement model
SF =~SE_1+SE_2+SE_3
CE =~ CE_PF + CE_P+ CE_G
B =~ a_habit + b_habit+ c_habit

# direct effect
B ~ c*CE
# mediator
SF ~  a*CE
B ~ b*SF

# indirect effect
ab := a*b
# total effect
total := c + (a*b)
'

fit1 <- sem(mediation.model, data = master_r, group="Location")
summary(fit1, fit.measures=TRUE)

fit2 <- sem(mediation.model, data = master_r, group="Location", group.equal = c("loadings"))
summary(fit2, fit.measures=TRUE)

In the analysis, I spotted that the measurement model (fit2) was significantly different from the basic configural model (fit1: all parameters were freely estimated across two groups). In this case, I wonder what are the steps I need do in my existing scripts before constraining the structural regression path coefficients to be equivalent in the two groups (Model 3), and later checking the validity of equality constraints to determine whether any of the constraints should be released in the final model (Model 4).

Thanks for the advice.

messages.subject: Re: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
You are missing the covariance between I and E factors

bifactor <- '
general =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts + c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts
internalizing =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts

externalizing =~c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts

internalizing ~~ externalizing
'

In a bifactor model, the general factor is not correlated with any other factor, but the specific factors are correlated between them

messages.body_plain:
One step further.

cfa() covaries all latents by default. So you also need:

general ~~ 0*externalizing + 0*internalizing

to identify the model.

Though looking at your content, it's a research area I'm familiar
with, and I'm skeptical a factor model is the way to go conceptually,
which could lead to estimation problems if the model is flat wrong.
But that's not really about lavaan.

messages.subject: Re: Starting values
messages.subject_clean: Starting values
messages.body_plain:
On 7/11/20 2:29 PM, Vera wrote:
> Dear all,
> I was wondering if anyone knows how the starting values of the
> parameters are guessed by lavaan?

- for factor loadings, lavaan using 'fabin3' estimates (see Hagglund,
1982); they are computed separately per factor

- for residuals variances of observed variances, lavaan uses the total
variance divided by two

- latent variances are set to 0.05

- everything else is zero

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Bivariate Parallel Process Modelling; Continuous and Ordinal variables
messages.subject_clean: Bivariate Parallel Process Modelling; Continuous and Ordinal variables
messages.body_plain:
Gopal:

(a) I do not see any problem combining a manifest growth curve with a latent growth curve in the same model.  You will need to declare the ordinal variable in order to include a threshold model for that variable.  In that sense, you will be modeling a latent variable, even though it does not look that way in your syntax.

(b) Combining three variables into one amounts to taking someone's position in a three dimensional space and representing it as a position in a one dimensional space.  If you are only interested in what these three variables share in common, then combining them may make sense (assuming that they have something in common).  If you are interested in what each of the three variables uniquely brings to the table, then combining them may throw away the information that interests you.

(c) Enter your model into lavaan and then try this command, substituting the name of your model where it says 'model'.

>lavaanify(model)

You will get a parameter table.  This is how lavaan represents your model.  If you scan across the column names, you will find a column labeled "ustart" for user start values.  These are likely mostly NA or zero.  However,  you can supply start values in this column and they will override the default start values used by lavaan.  (You can specify them in model syntax, see the online tutorial and model.syntax help file.)  These are the values at which estimation begins.  Specifying them can help reach a solution when estimation fails.  To make you guesses better than lavaan's guesses you want to draw from resources that lavaan does not have, like existing theory and past research.  If the model converges normally from the default start values, you probably do not need to worry about this.  However, you can try different start values just to confirm that you end up at the same solution.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

On Thursday, July 16, 2020 at 9:47:15 PM UTC+2, Nickname wrote:
> Gopal:
>
> (a) I do not see any problem combining a manifest growth curve with a latent growth curve in the same model.  You will need to declare the ordinal variable in order to include a threshold model for that variable.  In that sense, you will be modeling a latent variable, even though it does not look that way in your syntax.
>
> (b) Combining three variables into one amounts to taking someone's position in a three dimensional space and representing it as a position in a one dimensional space.  If you are only interested in what these three variables share in common, then combining them may make sense (assuming that they have something in common).  If you are interested in what each of the three variables uniquely brings to the table, then combining them may throw away the information that interests you.
>
> (c) Enter your model into lavaan and then try this command, substituting the name of your model where it says 'model'.
>
> >lavaanify(model)
>
> You will get a parameter table.  This is how lavaan represents your model.  If you scan across the column names, you will find a column labeled "ustart" for user start values.  These are likely mostly NA or zero.  However,  you can supply start values in this column and they will override the default start values used by lavaan.  (You can specify them in model syntax, see the online tutorial and model.syntax help file.)  These are the values at which estimation begins.  Specifying them can help reach a solution when estimation fails.  To make you guesses better than lavaan's guesses you want to draw from resources that lavaan does not have, like existing theory and past research.  If the model converges normally from the default start values, you probably do not need to worry about this.  However, you can try different start values just to confirm that you end up at the same solution.
>

messages.body_plain:
I think that if you were to have more items it would most likely work

A note about the fit measures, be careful for the interpretation of the RMSEA, as it favours larger models, so its easy to trick it into showing better fit by simple adding more parameters.

Previous research has shown that CFI and Gamma-Hat are less sensitive to characteristics like this, and mainly be sensitive to model misfit.

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

Now, my rant about the bifactor model. The reason I dont like is on how it is interpret, a basic constraint of the model is that the General factor is not correlated to the specific factors. So, as in your case you have externalization and internalization, for the model to make theoretical sense you would have to argue that the General factor is something that all the items share that is completely separate from externalization and internalization. Which then I dont understand how to make sense of that. Which for me its even weirder when use in Intelligence, as the have specific factors of cognitive performance (like executive function, visou-spatial, etc), and then set a General Intelligence factor, but if this general factor is uncorrelated to executive functions, how can I say that is Intelligence at all? For me these models make more theoretical sense as second order factors

Also, research has shown that the bifactor model simply fits better to random data, so it might just be a general factor structure that fits well without necessary being relevant (sorry I dont have those references at hand)

End rant

library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)
library(haven)
library(semTools)
DataG <- read_sav("C:/Users/kfls_/Google Drive/Freelancing/Ghada/New Analysis 13-7-20/R Analysis/DataG.sav")

ID_R =~ ID1 + ID2 + ID3 + ID4 + ID5
ID_C =~ ID6 + ID7 + ID8 + ID10

ID11*CORR3 + ID12*CORR3 + ID13*CORR3 + ID14*CORR3 + ID15*CORR3 +
ID16*CORR3 + ID17*CORR3

EO2 ~~ EO5
EO3 ~~ EO4
EO8 ~~ EO9
EO2 ~~ EO3
ID16 ~~ ID17
EO_C ~ ID_Sec + CORR_C + MODing
'

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your answer!  I have a question regarding the fabin3 estimates, are they only used for generating the starting values for the factor loadings or are they used in every iteration?

Op donderdag 16 juli 2020 20:07:30 UTC+2 schreef Yves Rosseel:

> On 7/11/20 2:29 PM, Vera wrote:
> > Dear all,
> > I was wondering if anyone knows how the starting values of the
> > parameters are guessed by lavaan?
>
> - for factor loadings, lavaan using 'fabin3' estimates (see Hagglund,
> 1982); they are computed separately per factor
>
> - for residuals variances of observed variances, lavaan uses the total
> variance divided by two
>
> - latent variances are set to 0.05
>
> - everything else is zero
>
> Yves.

messages.subject: Adjusting for Covariates in a Cross-Lagged Panel Model
messages.subject_clean: Adjusting for Covariates in a Cross-Lagged Panel Model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I was wondering if someone could advise on how to adjust a CLPM for simple covariates such as age and sex.

My CLPM takes this form:

cl_ld_1 <-
  '
#Regressions
FREQ_DEP_1 ~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 ~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0

#Covariances
FREQ_DEP_0 ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
FREQ_DEP_1~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1
'
fit_cl_ld_1 <- sem(cl_ld_1, data=d1, ordered=(' FREQ_DEP_1  '), estimator='PML', std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
summary(fit_cl_ld_1, fit.measures=T, standardized=T, rsquare=T)

To add in adjustment for age and sex, I was planning on adding covariances for age and sex with each of the variables at each time point. E.g. by doing the following:

cl_ld_2 <-
  '
#Regressions
FREQ_DEP_1~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 ~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0

#Covariances
FREQ_DEP_0 ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
FREQ_DEP_1~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1
AGE ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
AGE ~~ FREQ_DEP_0
SEX ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0
SEX ~~ FREQ_DEP_0
AGE ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1
AGE ~~ FREQ_DEP_1
SEX ~~ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1
SEX ~~ FREQ_DEP_1'

fit_cl_ld_2 <- sem(cl_ld_2, data=d1, ordered=('FREQ_DEP_1'), estimator='PML', std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, em.iter.max = 100)
summary(fit_cl_ld_2, fit.measures=T, standardized=T, rsquare=T)

Does that sound about right? or would a better approach be using regression equations?

Kind regards and much appreciation for any insights you can offer.

Angus

Hi,

Here's a small reproducible example in the context of adapting example of testing measurement invariance from the lavaan tutorial (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html):

#Specify model
cfaModel <- '
 visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'

#Measurement Invariance Syntax

                                           data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
                                           ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                                           group = "school")

configuralInvarianceSyntax <- as.character(configuralInvarianceModel)

#Summary of Model Features
summary(configuralInvarianceModel)

#Print Lavaan Syntax
cat(as.character(configuralInvarianceModel))

#Model Syntax in tabular form
lavaanify(cfaModel) #no error
lavaanify(configuralInvarianceSyntax) #ERROR
lavaanify(configuralInvarianceModel) #ERROR

  lavaan ERROR: wrong number of arguments in modifier (lambda.1_1.g1,lambda.1_1.g2) of element visual=~x1

messages.subject_clean: Sample Syntax for Second Order Multivariate Growth Curve with Covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello Awesome Lavaan Group!

I'm starting my dissertation analysis and am having trouble finding sample syntax for a more complex multivariate (i.e., parallel process) and second-order growth curve model.

My aim is to assess the impact of a host of predictors, both time-varying and time-invariant, on two growth trajectories that are modeled from second-order DVs at each time point. I have found many separate resources on how to model second-order growth curves, multivariate growth curves, and adding a single time-invariant or single time-varying covariate. Many questions arise when thinking about putting all of these different aspects together and expanding the number of covariates into a single model. I was hoping someone may have attempted a similar project successfully and would not mind sharing their code.

I really appreciate any and all help! Also, please let me know if this is not an appropriate question form for this google group as I have not used it before.

messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.subject_clean: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square...
Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.

If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however.

For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)

As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Sample Syntax for Second Order Multivariate Growth Curve with Covariates
messages.subject_clean: Sample Syntax for Second Order Multivariate Growth Curve with Covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Covariates:
You can include predictors which are time-variant by regressing the manifest variables directly onto them. if you have multiple covariates, simply keep adding them to the regression.

 manifest1_wave1 ~ covariate1_wave1 + covariate2_wave1 + ...
 manifest1_wave2 ~ covariate1_wave2+ covariate2_wave2 + ...

OR

intercept ~ covariate1 + covariate2 +...
slope ~ covariate1 + covariate2 +...

etc.

Time invariant predictors can be controlled for by putting them on the manifest or latent variables (though choice of which will change df and the model to some extent). It will "eat up" a lot of df to put them on the manifest variables, but some research questions will be better answered in this way.

Second-order curves & PPMs
The parallel process model (PPM) can be extended to second order, but depending on your research question this may or may not be ideal. You only capture whatever is common among those variables and will lose variance in each construct every time you group more things together.

That being said, you'll be able to modify/extend this:

model <-
'
## first order, putting together multiple constructs at each wave
constructA_wave1 =~ manifest1_wave1 + manifest2_wave1 + manifest3_wave1
constructB_wave1 =~ manifest4_wave1 + manifest5_wave1 + manifest6_wave1
constructC_wave1 =~ manifest7_wave1 + manifest8_wave1 + manifest9_wave1

constructA_wave2 =~ manifest1_wave2 + manifest2_wave2 + manifest3_wave2
constructB_wave2 =~ manifest4_wave2+ manifest5_wave2 + manifest6_wave2
constructC_wave2 =~ manifest7_wave2 + manifest8_wave2 + manifest9_wave2

etc. for more constructs/waves

##second order
wave1 =~ constructA_wave1 + constructB_wave1 + constructC_wave1
wave2 =~ constructA_wave2 + constructB_wave2 + constructC_wave2

 etc. for more waves

##Growth
Intercept =~ 1*wave1 + 1*wave2 + ... etc.
Slope =~ 0*wave1 + 1*wave2 + ... etc.
'

Keep in mind there are important specification rules for SEM & even more stringent ones for multilevel SEM.

I do not believe you will be able to test goodness of fit with only 2 waves of data, as I presented here. To see what you'll need, you can draw a path diagram and assess the number of df you have.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Sample Syntax for Second Order Multivariate Growth Curve with Covariates
messages.subject_clean: Sample Syntax for Second Order Multivariate Growth Curve with Covariates
messages.body_plain:
1. You can regress growth terms onto covariates OR wave by wave onto the manifest. I'm not sure if anyone has done a simulation comparing these, but ideologically the difference is what variance you are partialing out (in latent or manifest variables, respectively). See this resource for syntax on doing time variant vs. invariant (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html).

You are basically just going to take the code form here and use it two times (changing labels for the second construct) to go from a latent growth curve to a parallel process model.

re: the code you sent, Notice the `=~` operator is for measurement model (i.e., making the latent) and `~` is the regression.

2. Google: SEM specification rules, and look for pages like this (one of the first links: https://psu-psychology.github.io/psy-597-SEM/07_full_sem/full_sem_specification.html), but if you're doing a PPM that isn't second-order, you will be fine with 4 waves of data for two constructs and some exogenous covariates (up to and including quadratic models, I believe, but definitely linear).

2a. The correlation of the covariates occurs by default (as it would with multiple regression, too), but you could write it out if you wanted.

One more thing: Some people will not be a fan of this post-hoc removal of covariates, but some people are okay with it. Just report it if you do it.

"Any info on specifying the relationship between covariates for one process and across the two processes would be extremely helpful!" If I am understanding you correctly (correlations of covariates predicting 1 latent growth curve that is not predicting the other), this is all specified automatically. Without changing defaults which should only be changed with good reason, you do not need to specify anything.

messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.subject_clean: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi

As mentioned before, the RMSEA is a misfit per df, and in your models you have a lot of df to disperse it across. This is why RMSEA will tend to prefer larger models. Previous research has showns that CFI and Gamma-Hat are probably the best fit indices at being less sensitive to other sample/model characterictics. You can get gamma-hat from the moreFitIndices() function in semTools

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

On the other side, these are overall model fit evaluation, which has the limitation of possibly missed local misfit. So, after having "good" overall model fit you should also look at residuals and modification indices to evaluate if there is the need to add parameters to account for local misfit. The SRMR is the average bias in the residual correlations, so there might be some misfit related to specific items

Whittaker, T. A. (2012). Using the Modification Index and Standardized Expected Parameter Change for Model Modification. The Journal of Experimental Education, 80(1), 26–44. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299

Related to sample size and the chi-square, I am on the side that as a Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST), the chi square is designed to reject models with small amounts of misfit as sample size increases, so I in general dont pay attention too much to it.

Also, about the other fit indices (absolute, relative, or residuals), they were not designed to "accept" or "reject" a model like a NHST, they were designed as effect size metrics of misfit of the model (evaluated in different ways). But it has fallen into the common (bad) practice of using them as a NHST of "is a good model", but they should be answering "how much if the misfit of my model to represent the data?". On the same direction, the commonly used cutoffs for fit indices are not recommended as the recommended cutoffs come from specific research that does not allow to generalize them

Hope this helps

On Tuesday, July 21, 2020 at 10:21:49 AM UTC-5 christoph...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hello,
>
> This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square...
> Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.
>
> If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however.
>
> For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)
>
> As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).
>
> Best,
> Chris

Some argue that in large samples (does mine qualify as large, for such a statement?) even small and substantively unimportant differences between the estimated model and the ‘true’ underlying model will result in rejection of the model that is tested. Do you guys think I should reject my model or do you think it seems fine?
> >
> > My fit indices are as follows:
> >
> >
> >
> > Thank you in advance!
> >
> > Best.

cl_ld_2 <-
  '

# LVs
phase_0 =~ CHRONO_0 + getup_0
phase_1 =~ CHRONO_1 + getup_1

#Regressions
phase_1 ~ phase_0 + LOG_avLight
LOG_avLight_1 ~ phase_0 + LOG_avLight

#Covariances
phase_0 ~~ LOG_avLight
phase_1 ~~ LOG_avLight_1
'
fit_cl_ld_2 <- sem(cl_ld_2, data=d1, ordered=c('CHRONO_0', 'CHRONO_1', 'GET_UP_0','GET_UP_1'), estimator='PML',std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)

Any idea why this might be the case? I have successfully done this with a very similar model that also uses ordinal variables to indicate the latent variables.

messages.subject: Re: Failed Convergence: Latent Variables in CLPM
messages.subject_clean: Failed Convergence: Latent Variables in CLPM
messages.body_plain:
It is likely that your model is underidentified, especially with only
two indicators per factor, and those categorical. In particular,
phase_1 is probably not identified. Try constraining the two phase
variables to measurement invariance (loadings and thresholds).
std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE is also probably not what you want for longitudinal data.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.subject_clean: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.body_plain:
Joost,

Those are some very large modification indices.

The first one. ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB6_14, looks like the same item at two timepoints. It is usually not controversial to allow disturbance covariances in that situation, even if it is post hoc.

Further, most of the large residuals involve variable B6. Before making any changes, I suggest you check the residuals in your model to get a better grasp of what's going on with it.

And finally, and this will worsen fit, CLPMs usually impose metric invariance longitudinally. It's not clear what information you'll get out of this otherwise. I'm surprised the VariableA_14 portion of the model was identified without it.

Pat

> Dear Mauricio,
>
> This very much helps, indeed! Thank you for taking the time to comment. Greatly appreciated.
>
> df is high because I am using 4 latent variables, for 2 constructs at 2 time points. Variable A is measured using the same 2 items at 10 and 14 years. Variable B is measured using the same 7 items at 10 and 14 years. All the items are ordered.
>
> This is the unadjusted model I am currently using:
> Model1.0 <- '
>

> VariableA_10 =~ ItemA1_10 + ItemA2_10
> VariableB_10 =~ ItemB1_10 + ItemB2_10 + ItemB3_10 + ItemB4_10 + ItemB5_10 + ItemB6_10 + ItemB7_10

> VariableB_14 =~ ItemB1_14 + ItemB2_14 + ItemB3_14 + ItemB4_14 + ItemB5_14 + ItemB6_14 + ItemB7_14
>

> VariableB_14 ~ VariableB_10 + VariableA_10
>
> # Covariances
> VariableA_10 ~~ VariableB_10
> '
>
> Based on the modification indices and residuals, there indeed seems to be some local misfit.
> For example modificationindices(mymodelfit.model1.0, sort.= TRUE, minimum.value = 20) returns:
>
>                     lhs op           rhs      mi           epc     sepc.lv <http://sepc.lv>   sepc.all sepc.nox
>
> 291 ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB6_14   166.243  0.325   0.325    0.482    0.482
>
> 255 ItemB3_10 ~~ ItemB6_14   109.582  0.224   0.224    0.536    0.536
>

>
> 337 ItemB6_14 ~~ ItemB7_14     80.766  0.241   0.241    0.433    0.433
>
> 283 ItemB6_10 ~~ ItemB7_10     77.666  0.257   0.257    0.468    0.468
>
> Do you think I should correlate these measurement residuals or make any other adjustments to my model? I am hesitant to make post-hoc adjustments to the model.
>
> Thanks again!
>
> Best,
>
> Joost
>
> Op dinsdag 21 juli 2020 22:41:40 UTC+2 schreef Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal:
> > Hi
> >
> > As mentioned before, the RMSEA is a misfit per df, and in your models you have a lot of df to disperse it across. This is why RMSEA will tend to prefer larger models. Previous research has showns that CFI and Gamma-Hat are probably the best fit indices at being less sensitive to other sample/model characterictics. You can get gamma-hat from the moreFitIndices() function in semTools
> >
> > Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864
> >
> > Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224
> >
> > On the other side, these are overall model fit evaluation, which has the limitation of possibly missed local misfit. So, after having "good" overall model fit you should also look at residuals and modification indices to evaluate if there is the need to add parameters to account for local misfit. The SRMR is the average bias in the residual correlations, so there might be some misfit related to specific items
> >
> > Whittaker, T. A. (2012). Using the Modification Index and Standardized Expected Parameter Change for Model Modification. The Journal of Experimental Education, 80(1), 26–44. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299
> >
> > Related to sample size and the chi-square, I am on the side that as a Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST), the chi square is designed to reject models with small amounts of misfit as sample size increases, so I in general dont pay attention too much to it.
> >
> > Also, about the other fit indices (absolute, relative, or residuals), they were not designed to "accept" or "reject" a model like a NHST, they were designed as effect size metrics of misfit of the model (evaluated in different ways). But it has fallen into the common (bad) practice of using them as a NHST of "is a good model", but they should be answering "how much if the misfit of my model to represent the data?". On the same direction, the commonly used cutoffs for fit indices are not recommended as the recommended cutoffs come from specific research that does not allow to generalize them
> >
> > Hope this helps
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 21, 2020 at 10:21:49 AM UTC-5 christoph...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square...
> > > Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.
> > >
> > > If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however.
> > >
> > > For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)
> > >
> > > As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Chris
> > > On Tuesday, July 21, 2020 at 1:00:45 AM UTC-7 Joost G wrote:
> > > > Dear all,
> > > >
> > > > I am running a CLPM in Lavaan, to explore a possible bidirectional association between two variables, measured at two time points. Its part of a longitudinal study. I include ~3300 children in this specific analysis and adjust for covariates in 3 incremental steps/models.
> > > >
> > > > However, I have doubts on the accuracy of my model. CFI, RMSEA and SRMR seem good. However, my Chi-square is quite large. This is where I'd like your input. Some argue that in large samples (does mine qualify as large, for such a statement?) even small and substantively unimportant differences between the estimated model and the ‘true’ underlying model will result in rejection of the model that is tested. Do you guys think I should reject my model or do you think it seems fine?
> > > >
> > > > My fit indices are as follows:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thank you in advance!
> > > >
> > > > Best.

messages.subject_clean: Failed Convergence: Latent Variables in CLPM
messages.body_plain:
Measurement invariance for categorical indicators is most commonly
defined as loading and threshold invariance simultaneously.

So loadings looks something like this:

phase_0 =~ 1*CHRONO_0 + l1*getup_0
phase_1 =~ 1*CHRONO_1 + l1*getup_1

That still may not identify it, depending on other details--there
might need to be some additional constraints on l1.

I don't have a lot of experience with manipulating thresholds in
lavaan, but they use a | syntax for each ordinal variable. Online
tutorials or someone else here should be able to help with that
syntax.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.subject_clean: Model Fit Indices - Hows my model?
messages.body_plain:
Oh, Ok, its a panel model

I would recommend to look at these modifications on the measurement model, without regressions yet.

Also, in models like this is common to add all the disturbance covariances for the same item over time. This would be saying that there is something common between the same item over time that is above and beyond the relation between factors. Which is not hard to argue.

Next, if you were to still have large mi and spec.all, you should also have to consider if the modification makes theoretical sense and you can justify it? By adding a disturbance covariance, you are saying that there is something in common between those 2 indicators above and beyond the relations between factors, can you argue that for those added parameters. An issue with modification indices is that that can get out of control by adding parameters that would help the model but are not relevant. Remember SEM is a theory based approach, so by adding any modification you would be recommending future researchers to add those same parameters

If the items are ordered, are you treating them as such? Ans using WLS?

> > Op dinsdag 21 juli 2020 22:41:40 UTC+2 schreef Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal:
> > > Hi
> > >
> > > As mentioned before, the RMSEA is a misfit per df, and in your models you have a lot of df to disperse it across. This is why RMSEA will tend to prefer larger models. Previous research has showns that CFI and Gamma-Hat are probably the best fit indices at being less sensitive to other sample/model characterictics. You can get gamma-hat from the moreFitIndices() function in semTools
> > >
> > > Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864
> > >
> > > Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224
> > >
> > > On the other side, these are overall model fit evaluation, which has the limitation of possibly missed local misfit. So, after having "good" overall model fit you should also look at residuals and modification indices to evaluate if there is the need to add parameters to account for local misfit. The SRMR is the average bias in the residual correlations, so there might be some misfit related to specific items
> > >
> > > Whittaker, T. A. (2012). Using the Modification Index and Standardized Expected Parameter Change for Model Modification. The Journal of Experimental Education, 80(1), 26–44. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299
> > >
> > > Related to sample size and the chi-square, I am on the side that as a Null Hypothesis Significance Test (NHST), the chi square is designed to reject models with small amounts of misfit as sample size increases, so I in general dont pay attention too much to it.
> > >
> > > Also, about the other fit indices (absolute, relative, or residuals), they were not designed to "accept" or "reject" a model like a NHST, they were designed as effect size metrics of misfit of the model (evaluated in different ways). But it has fallen into the common (bad) practice of using them as a NHST of "is a good model", but they should be answering "how much if the misfit of my model to represent the data?". On the same direction, the commonly used cutoffs for fit indices are not recommended as the recommended cutoffs come from specific research that does not allow to generalize them
> > >
> > > Hope this helps
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, July 21, 2020 at 10:21:49 AM UTC-5 christoph...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Hello,
> > > >
> > > > This certainly is a large enough sample to magnify a small amount of misfit based on your sample size, but that is a large chi square...
> > > > Your other fit indices are good, but 'how good' depends on the importance of your research question. In my opinion, these are decent fit indices and I wouldn't think twice if this were for anything less than publication. Given a few persistent researchers are stubborn about significant chi-square, I would try and better fit the model to the data if I were publishing. Without a third wave to try an RICLPM model, I'm not sure how you would do that, however.
> > > >
> > > > If this isn't your cup of tea, you can do some research on Hoelter's N, which was invented to tell you what number of participants would make your model's chi square significant (because power works "against you" in SEM). if you call fitmeasures(model_fit, "cn_05"), you will get a number for your model at p = 0.05 significance level. A rule of thumb (used by Hoelter, at least) was 200+ indicates it's "okay" that your chi square is significant (with ML or MLR), but I have not personally found a simulation study of the exact number. Either way, it's "not interpretable" when chi-square isn't significant, according to many. I want to point out that some very well respected researchers (e.g., Hu & Bentler) do not recommend using this, however.
> > > >
> > > > For more information about what specific fit indices should be, you should think about what the formula for that index is, for example RMSEA is fit (or misfit) per df, so (for example) RMSEA is often artificially better in models with large numbers of df than other models. More information on both can be found and easily interpreted here (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm)
> > > >
> > > > As an aside, this is mainly a forum for technical questions about lavaan, not general SEM questions, even if it gets used as both. But, admittedly, I have been the guy asking general SEM questions before, which is why I took the time to answer this one and free up time of the smarter minds of Yves and Terrence, haha).
> > > >
> > > > Best,

Some argue that in large samples (does mine qualify as large, for such a statement?) even small and substantively unimportant differences between the estimated model and the ‘true’ underlying model will result in rejection of the model that is tested. Do you guys think I should reject my model or do you think it seems fine?

messages.body_plain:
I am using Multiple imputation data to fit parallel models. I have checked variable models individually to ensure best fit but when I combine some of the variables into a parallel model I get this error (
Error in D3.LRT(object, h1 = h1, useImps = useImps, asymptotic = asymptotic, : D3 test statistic could not be calculated. Try the D2 pooling method.), which I am not sure what it means, or how to fix it.

Another few questions:
1- After plotting some of my variables I see that there is a positive trend and then a decline afterward, as well as extremely large variability in response within same participant. Would this lead to negative variances in time points and/or slope & intercept variance? Do I need to worry about that? Would this be considered a Heywood case as well?

2- This might be a silly question but I don't quite understand why to models that are perfectly fitted when analyzed individually lead to a bad fit when combined into a parallel model. What should I do in this case? Some of my data is extremely variable as a group as well as within the same participant, how do you deal with this issue? I've tried every different possibility  in order to get the best fit (i.e. quadratics, picewise, etc.)

3- Is also not uncommon  that when running parallel growth models with multiple imputed data I might get:
Negative test statistic set to zero

Negative pooled test statistic was set to zero, so fit will appear to be arbitrarily perfect.

Why is that? How do I fix this? Should I worry about overfitting if my RMSEA=0, CFI=1 etc?

Any help on this would be much appreciated!

messages.subject_clean: Conducting a CFA on bi-factor models
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I would like to conduct a CFA on a bi-factor model of the TAS-20 but have run into some problems interpreting the output. My code and the model fit was good, however, I noticed that I did not get any factor loadings for the EOT subscale, the variance for the EOT subscale was negative, and the R squared values for items 15 and 16 were negative. This is odd because I tested other models on the TAS-20 using the same set of data but haven't come across any negative variances or R squared values. Is this an issue with the code or the data?

This is the code I used:
TAS20_model6 <- 'DIF =~ TAS20_1 + TAS20_3 + TAS20_6 + TAS20_7 + TAS20_9 + TAS20_13 + TAS20_14
                 DDF =~ TAS20_2 + TAS20_4_R + TAS20_11 + TAS20_12 + TAS20_17
                 EOT =~ TAS20_5_R + TAS20_8 + TAS20_10_R + TAS20_15 + TAS20_16 + TAS20_18_R + TAS20_19_R + TAS20_20
                 method =~ TAS20_4_R + TAS20_5_R + TAS20_10_R + TAS20_18_R + TAS20_19_R

                gen_alexi =~ TAS20_1 + TAS20_3 + TAS20_6 + TAS20_7 + TAS20_9 + TAS20_13 + TAS20_14 + #DIF
                              TAS20_2 + TAS20_4_R + TAS20_11 + TAS20_12 + TAS20_17 + #DDF
                              TAS20_5_R + TAS20_8 + TAS20_10_R + TAS20_15 + TAS20_16 + TAS20_18_R + TAS20_19_R + TAS20_20 #EOT

                   DIF ~~ DDF
                   DIF ~~ EOT
                   DDF ~~ EOT

                   gen_alexi =~ 0*DIF + 0*DDF + 0*EOT + 0*method'

TAS20_model6_fit <- cfa(TAS20_model6,
                        data = final_data_sg,
                        estimator = "MLM",
                        orthogonal = FALSE,
                        std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE)

summary(TAS20_model6_fit,
        fit.measures = TRUE,
        standardized = TRUE,
        rsquare = TRUE)

Please let me know if you have any clue what went wrong. Thank you very much!

messages.body_plain:
Sarah

Right now the best recommendation with lavaan would be to use the indicator product terms.
1. You create mean center indicator product terms, or residualized indicator product terms. Can use the function indProd() from semTools for this
2. Include these indicator product terms into the latent regression in lavaan reacting a new Interaction factor defined by the product indicators
3. Run the latent regression with the Latent interaction terms, this way you can evaluate the interaction regression slope, and increase in R2 by adding it
4. Probe simple intercepts and slopes for the interactions, can use the probe2WayRC (for the residualize indicators) or probe2WayMC (for the mean center indicators), functions from semTools
5. Plot the simple slopes to visualize the effect of the interactions, with plotProbe function from semTools

In the helps page of each function you can see examples

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: Conducting a CFA on bi-factor models
messages.subject_clean: Conducting a CFA on bi-factor models
messages.body_plain:
Joan,

At a guess your biggest problem is that this

 gen_alexi =~ 0*DIF + 0*DDF + 0*EOT + 0*method

should be

 gen_alexi ~~ 0*DIF + 0*DDF + 0*EOT + 0*method
 method ~~ 0*DIF + 0*DDF + 0*EOT

As written, it's specifying a second-order factor (not a bifactor)
with loadings fixed to zero, and isn't constraining the method factor
to be uncorrelated with the content factors.

Once you fix those things, you may continue to have problems with both
gen_alexi and method in the model, but one step at a time.

Pat

messages.subject_clean: mediation analysis with categorical variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Paul.

First, your tables are difficult to read--can you post them in either plain-text for a fixed-width font, please?

Second, in a parallel mediation case, it's standard practice to let all of the disturbances of the mediators covary with each other. Otherwise you're incorporating the strong hypothesis that medul is the only cause of the relations among them.

If I'm reading right, that will saturate your model and make the structural relations unfalsifiable, but it's the best I've got.

Pat

messages.subject: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statment?
messages.subject_clean: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statment?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm curious if lavaan has something similar to the Mplus "within" command.  The within command designates a continuous level 1 variable has having no variance and no covariance at level 2. (Conversely, the "between" command stipulates no variance at level 1.)  Without the within command, any level 1 variable also has a level 2 variance and covariance, even if that variable is not included in the between structure. This behavior is also the default in lavaan.

Now it's easy enough to set the between variance to zero for the level 1 variable in question, but that changes model df.  In addition, the between covariance matrix still features the level 2 variance and covariances for the variable in question, which has ramifications for model fit stats. The Mplus within command retains the level 1 variable in the between covariance matrix but the variance and covariances for the variable are all zero.

Happy to provide a reproducible example if needed.  Thanks in advance.

Joe

messages.body_plain:
In this case, since one of your variables is a single, dichotomous, observed variables you might be able to use multiple group modeling instead of product indicator terms. If the dichotomous variable is the moderator, you can use that variable as the grouping variable and see if the X->Y path differs across groups (this would be evidence of moderation).

Alex

On Thursday, July 23, 2020 at 12:57:33 AM UTC-4 mauga...@gmail.com wrote:
> Sarah
>
> Right now the best recommendation with lavaan would be to use the indicator product terms.
> 1. You create mean center indicator product terms, or residualized indicator product terms. Can use the function indProd() from semTools for this
> 2. Include these indicator product terms into the latent regression in lavaan reacting a new Interaction factor defined by the product indicators
> 3. Run the latent regression with the Latent interaction terms, this way you can evaluate the interaction regression slope, and increase in R2 by adding it
> 4. Probe simple intercepts and slopes for the interactions, can use the probe2WayRC (for the residualize indicators) or probe2WayMC (for the mean center indicators), functions from semTools
> 5. Plot the simple slopes to visualize the effect of the interactions, with plotProbe function from semTools
>
> In the helps page of each function you can see examples
>
> Hope this helps
>

messages.body_plain:
Negative covariance is a big deal and you need to fix it because the model is NOT admissible.

there are a number of strategies

1. there may be an item or latent variable that has negative error variance causing the covariance matrix not to be positive definite. find and correct it to a small number above zero.

2. you potentially have too many factors. look at the correlation values. if close to 1.00 or >1.00 you know those 2 factors need to be joined together

3. force some of the covariances not to be negative --i have the least experience with doing that.

messages.subject_clean: Warning message: trouble constructing W matrix; used generalized inverse for A11 submatrix
messages.body_plain:
I had the same error message and went to read the Muthen 1984 paper referenced in the error message (A general SEM with dichotomous, ordered categorical, and continuous latent variable indicators).

This is what I gathered (Pp. 119-120. )
W is a positive definite weight matrix used at the third estimation stage. Is part of the weighted least squares fitting function which is miminized by the estimation. Forming this matrix is needed to obtain a limited information generalized least squares estimator.
The A(g) submatrix is a “consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the estimator Theta prime”. Theta (not primed) is the “vector of free and distinct model parameters”
For me the problem came from the fact that I had specified condition.x=FALSE in the lavaan fitting command. I had a dichotomous observed exogenous variable X, so I was using the WLSMV estimator. This requires condition.x=TRUE for models with categorical covariates. So if my understanding is correct, this created a problem in relation to third stage estimation.

You did not list the fitting command you used and your estimator so I am not sure if this applies to you as well. Here is something on the Mplus website that explains why conditioning on X observed covariates is important - if this applies to you (but the post dates back to 2018) or to someone else who might read this post because of the same error message.

https://www.statmodel.com/download/Covariates%20%E2%80%93%20analysis%20conditioned%20on%20covariates.pdf

Myriam

messages.body_plain:
I am doing parallel analyses with my latent growth models and after plotting some of my variables I see that there is a positive trend and then a decline afterward, as well as extremely large variability in response within same participant. Would this lead to negative variances in time points and/or slope & intercept variance? Do I need to worry about that? Would this be considered a Heywood case as well?

This might be a silly question but I don't quite understand why to models that are perfectly fitted when analyzed individually lead to a bad fit when combined into a parallel model. What should I do in this case? Some of my data is extremely variable as a group as well as within the same participant, how do you deal with this issue? I've tried every different possibility  in order to get the best fit (i.e. quadratics, picewise, etc.)

Is also not uncommon  that when running parallel growth models with multiple imputed data I might get:
Negative test statistic set to zero

Negative pooled test statistic was set to zero, so fit will appear to be arbitrarily perfect.

Should I worry about overfitting here? what does this mean?

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I specifically specified that

G_EOT ~~  0* N_DIF + 0* P_DIF + 0*N_DDF + 0*P_DDF
N_DIF ~~ 0*P_DDF
P_DIF ~~ 0*N_DDF

because I was using the method that you taught me to test a bi-factor model for the PAQ. Before you taught me that method, I had used gen_alexi =~  0* N_DIF + 0* P_DIF + 0*N_DDF + 0*P_DDF + 0*G_EOT. However, after I changed it to gen_alex ~~  0* N_DIF + 0* P_DIF + 0*N_DDF + 0*P_DDF + 0*G_EOT, it allowed N_DIF to correlate with P_DDF, and P_DIF to correlate with N_DDF, which is not what we want in the model. Hence, I added in N_DIF ~~ 0*P_DDF and
P_DIF ~~ 0*N_DDF, to ensure that the model is specified correctly (see the attached picture of the model we are trying to test).

I have copied and pasted the code that I have used and the output below. Hopefully this provides some clarity. Thank you very much for your help.

Are you using categorical data? Then this is normal, as the default DWLS
estimator has no likelihood.

If you are using continuous data + ML, this should not happen. In that
case, please send me a reproducible example (script + data), or open an
github issue.

Yves.

On 7/24/20 5:40 PM, bbj...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi All,
>
> I'm curious if lavaan has something similar to the Mplus "within"
> command.  The within command designates a continuous level 1 variable
> has having no variance and no covariance at level 2. (Conversely, the
> "between" command stipulates no variance at level 1.)  Without the
> within command, any level 1 variable also has a level 2 variance and
> covariance, even if that variable is not included in the between
> structure. This behavior is also the default in lavaan.
>
> Now it's easy enough to set the between variance to zero for the level 1
> variable in question, but that changes model df.  In addition, the
> between covariance matrix still features the level 2 variance and
> covariances for the variable in question, which has ramifications for
> model fit stats. The Mplus within command retains the level 1 variable
> in the between covariance matrix but the variance and covariances for
> the variable are all zero.
>
> Happy to provide a reproducible example if needed.  Thanks in advance.
>
> Joe
