messages.body_plain:
Joan,

You've asked about multiple models, sometimes in the same thread. I corrected myself in the July 13 thread to mean only gen_alexineeded to be orthogonal to (uncorrelated with) the five specific factors. The specific factors do not need to be orthogonal to each other.

As far as:

"
it allowed N_DIF to correlate with P_DDF, and P_DIF to correlate with N_DDF, which is not what we want in the model. Hence, I added in N_DIF ~~ 0*P_DDF and
P_DIF ~~ 0*N_DDF, to ensure that the model is specified correctly (see the attached picture of the model we are trying to test). "

Without more context for what you're trying to do, we have no idea about that. But the diagram you attached (thank you) shows N_DIF, P_DIF, N_DDF, and P_DDF all intercorrelated.

Another issue is that you use the same indicator as the scaling indicator for both N_DDF and gen_alex , which I think is not recommended in bifactor models. I suggest fixing the variance of gen_alex to 1 and freeing the loading of PAQ_1 on gen_alex.

But on the upside, you do not have any negative variance estimates or latent variable standardized covariances (correlations) greater than one.

Can you provide:

lavInspect(PAQ_model6_fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>") . Also, please use a fixed-width font when posting tables to the list so the column headers line up.

But I don't think it will show anything obvious. I suspect the problem is either a mis-specified model due to the omitted covariances, or an empirically underidentified model due to the size of the model relative to the sample.

Pat

Hm. The 'usual' way is by using standardizedSolution(). But this does

If your model is scale-invariant, you may get close by using both std.lv <http://std.lv>
= TRUE (which you already do) and std.ov = TRUE.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Any work-around for inability to get "casewise" residuals in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Any work-around for inability to get "casewise" residuals in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Thank you for this! I also performed a path analysis in lavaan based on observed variables. This code was exactly what I needed to calculate my casewise model residuals!

It seems that the following adaptation to my data and model was successful. I was able to run it and obtained a residual data matrix. (Note to other beginners like me: I had to make sure that all my variables were as.numeric. I also created a subset data frame with only my model variables and in the exact order in which they appear below - but maybe that was overkill).

I have two questions to obtain additional information through this procedure.

Would it be possible to know how to adapt the syntax to obtain standardized residuals?

Also, is there a way to obtain Cook values through this easy procedure? I am not really familiar with matrix algebra and I only recently started using R and lavaan.

Here is the adapted code:

In my model, I have 2 exogenous variables, 3 mediators, and 2 outcomes (1 is binary, so I used WLSMV).  So: X1, X2, M1, M2, M3, Y1, Y2

predictors <- c("X1", "X2","M1", "M2", "M3")

outcomes <- c("M1", "M2", "M3","Y1", "Y2")

X <- as.matrix(mydata[predictors])

X <- cbind(intercept = 1,  X)

Y <- as.matrix(mydata[outcomes])

B <- lavInspect(mymodelfit, "coef")$beta[outcomes, predictors]

int <- lavInspect(mymodelfit, "coef")$alpha[outcomes, "intercept"]

B <- t(cbind(intercept = int, B))

Y.hat <- X %*% B # regression equation

E <- Y - Y.hat   # casewise residuals

Thank you again!

Myriam

Update on my previous post:

I realized that obtaining standardized residuals was just a matter of basic stats : (Residuals - Mean of residuals)/SD of residuals. Here is my code for other beginners like me. (Now that I think about it, I could have used a standardize function.)

#inputing residuals back into data frame

mydata$M1.resid <- E[ , "M1"]

#standardizing residuals

mydata$M1.zres <- as.numeric(

              (mydata$M1.resid-mean(mydata$M1.resid))

                /sd(mydata$M1.resid))

Remaining question:
I am still wondering if there is a way to obtain Cook's distance.

I will look back at my stat textbooks, but if someone has an easy way to obtain them, I would be super grateful.

Thank you!
Myriam

messages.subject: Syntax for formative constructs
messages.subject_clean: Syntax for formative constructs
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan community,

At the moment, I am working on testing my second order model. The goodness of fit for model appears to be good (n = 168; CFI = .978; TLI = .975; RMSEA = .028; SRMR = .059)

Model Test User Model:
                                               Standard      Robust
  Test Statistic                                240.947     227.373
  Degrees of freedom                                201         201
  P-value (Chi-square)                            0.028       0.098
  Scaling correction factor                                   1.060

Overall_model<-'
                ELDIR =~ ELDIR2 + ELDIR4 + ELDIR5 + ELDIR7 + ELDIR8
                ELDIR7 ~~ ELDIR8
                ELDIP =~ ELDIP1 + ELDIP2 + ELDIP3 + ELDIP4 + ELDIP6
                SNFER=~ SNFER1 + SNFER2 + SNFER3 + SNFER4 + SNFER5
                                SNFER1 ~~ SNFER2
                SNFEC =~ SNFEC1 + SNFEC2  + SNFEC4
                SNFEA =~ SNFEA2 + SNFEA3 + SNFEA4Rev+ SNFEA5

                ELDI =~ ELDIR + ELDIP
                SNFE =~ SNFER + SNFEC + SNFEA
                ELDI ~ SNFE'

model1<-sem(Overall_model, data=data,  estimator="MLR", missing="FIML")
summary(model1, fit.measures=TRUE, rsquare=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

However, as the author of one research instrument for ELDIR and ELDIP does not provide enough information, I have second thoughts that his instrument might be of a formative nature (i.e. All items imply on different actions and might not be considered interchangeable). The author reports his usage of AMOS while I have read that this software cannot properly handle formative constructs. Therefore, I am searching for options to adjust my syntax for using the constructs of ELDIR and ELDIP as formative ones. The goal is to understand whether both factors should be used as formative or reflective.

Before writing, I have read all threads about formative constructs; however, since I am new to lavaan, I have not found them to be useful. Apart from the operator "<~" that doed not seem to work, I have not found anything useful; therefore, I would appreciate any comments or suggestions.

Many thanks in advance.

Regards,
Artem

messages.subject_clean: How to resolve an issue using the FIML function?
messages.body_plain:
I am currently analyzing my data for my thesis research, and an issue has come up that we do not know how to resolve. I have two time points, and I am conducting various path analyses in R with lavaan installed.

The issue I am having is with accounting for missing data. Since this is a longitudinal study, only 66% of participants completed both time points. I know that the default estimator with the lavaan package is maximum likelihood. However, this estimator removes cases that did not complete both time points from my analyses. Therefore, I resorted to use full information maximum likelihood estimator. However, when I use the function (missing = “ML”), my results come out strange. For instance, my r-square results are abnormally high, and my parameter estimates become very different from the default estimator and are very large as well. We think something isn’t right with my missing data function.

Does anyone know what might be causing this issue? Is there a better way to account for missing data in my longitudinal design with the lavaan package in R?

Your help and advice is greatly appreciated, as I feel like I am hitting a wall right now.  Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yves,

Thanks for your reply.  I think there are some discrepancies in the two approaches but I could be wrong.  Here's a reproducible example using data from the Mplus users guide. The within level has simple mediation model in which x2 mediates the relationship between x1 and y.  The variable x1 is within only, as it is not included in the between-level structure.  Variable w is included in the between-level structure but not within.  Mplus syntax would have x1 identified as "within" and w as "between."

mp9.3.dat <- read.table("https://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap9/ex9.3.dat")
names(mp9.3.dat) <- c("u", "y", "x1", "x2", "w", "clus")

mp9.3.l <- '
level: 1
y ~ x2
x2 ~ x1

level: 2
y ~ x2 + w
'

$within

y   1.261
x2  0.443  0.964
x1 -0.009 -0.019  1.039

$clus

y   0.757
x2 -0.034  0.021
w   0.576 -0.003  1.008

> med.9.3.out$results$model$sampstat$BETWEEN$covariances
       Y     X2 X1  W
Y   0.76     NA NA NA
X2 -0.03  0.019 NA NA
X1  0.00  0.000  0 NA
W   0.58 -0.002  0  1

> med.9.3.out$results$model$sampstat$WITHIN$covariances
      Y     X2 X1  W
Y  1.26     NA NA NA
X2 0.44  0.965 NA NA
X1 0.23 -0.021  1 NA
W  0.00  0.000  0  0

For the most part, the parameter estimates are the same or close, but the number of estimated free parameters isn't the same.  Model chi-square, baseline chi-square, CFI and RMSEA are the same across the two programs but not SRMR (at both levels) and TLI.  I've attached Mplus output for your perusal.  Thanks in advance for having a look.

Best,

Joe

messages.subject_clean: How to resolve an issue using the FIML function?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jessica

The problem with FIML and any other imputation method (In My Opinion) is that they maximise the start values (M, SD, covariance & correlation matrices) of the known values before fitting the model. This inflates the model to correspond to the full data.

Recommended limits on imputation are 5% missing from Little & Rubin, whereas I’ve made a career habit of allowing 10% missing. After that we have no way of knowing if the missing is psychologically true when imputed. Even though the algorithm will work with very high % of missing data. It just doesn't mean it's true.

My strategy is always to conduct MVA outside SEM (I use EM) and decide which participants to keep and impute by inspecting the impact of MVA before analysis.

I think the problem you have identified is because you are imputing too much missing without checking that it is valid.

In repeated measures the best you can hope for is to save people who missed only a little data and accept that your working dataset will be much smaller than 100%

Little, R. J. A., & Rubin, D. B. (2002). Statistical analysis with missing data (2nd ed.). Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons.

messages.subject: Re: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statment?
messages.subject_clean: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statment?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Joseph,

> What I find interesting is that the observed covariance matrices do not
> have the same structure at the different levels (which seems an obvious
> point): within has x1, x2, and y, and between has w, x2, and y.  Mplus,
> however, includes w at the within level and x1 at the between (with zero
> variance and covariance for each).

That is just a matter of presentation. Internally, lavaan is using the
same matrices as Mplus. But only when we need to combine the two levels
(for computing the loglikelihood) do we 'extend' the matrices to contain
all within+between variables.

> For the most part, the parameter estimates are the same or close, but
> the number of estimated free parameters isn't the same.

I believe the difference is due to this Mplus warning:

*** WARNING in MODEL command
   In the MODEL command, the following variable is an x-variable on the
BETWEEN
   level and a y-variable on the WITHIN level.  This variable will be
treated
   as a y-variable on both levels:  X2

lavaan is not doing this (yet?). This is indeed a difference. However,
my impression is that Mplus is in fact always using 'fixed.x = FALSE'
when estimating the parameters, but then selectively hides 'exogenous'
fixed.x parameters from the output by default. If you mention them
explicitly in the model specification, the number of free parameter
changes, but the output remains identical:

   MODEL:
     %WITHIN%
       y ON x2;
       x2 ON x1;
       x1;
     %BETWEEN%
       y ON x2 w;

       w;

So to get output closer to that of Mplus (in terms of parameter
estimates), you can use

fit <- sem(mp9.3.l, data=mp9.3.dat, cluster="clus", fixed.x = FALSE)

The default (in lavaan) is fixed.x = TRUE, and in this case (unlike
Mplus) the exogenous means/variances/covariances are truly fixed to
their sample values. This often leads to small but noticeable differences.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
For future reference, it would also be helpful to show us the results of cfa(), not just summary(). What did the top of summary() show you, specifically the fit measures?

But here it's easy--your model is unidentified. In most circumstances in a CFA, you need at least three indicators per factor unless you have additional constraints to compensate. SAR and PER each have only two. There's not enough information in the original variance/covariance matrix to estimate this model.

That said, if, as I'd guess, SAR1 and SAR2 are theoretically interchangeable, and likewise for PER1 and PER2, it's probably defensible to do this:

SAR =~ 1*SAR1 + 1*SAR2
PER =~ 1*PER1 + 1*PER2

With the rest the same. this constrains the two loadings on each first-order factor to be equal, which is a possible "additional constraint" I mentioned.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
It's hard to tell all of what's going on here, but you almost certainly don't want to "standardize" all of the latent growth terms.

Since the Is and Ss have their loadings defined, what you've done in the "lv as scaling" section is constrain the variances of all of your latent intercepts to equality over variables and constrain all of the slopes to zero growth/flat over time.

I suggest you try building up from a smaller model until you've got something that works before going to all 10 (!) parallel processes.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

Progress!

You still need to remove the additional covariance constraints between N_DIF and P_DDF and between P_DIF and N_DDF if you want it to match the diagram you sent.

At this point, though, I doubt it will resolve the warning.

The two principal remaining sources of the warning are:

1) Mis-specified model (possibly related to the orthogonality of G_EOT)
2) Too small sample for the model and variance-covariances.

But note that is a warning, not an error. If adjusting the model doesn't resolve it, and considering there's no obvious inadmissibility, I would next check the model fit. If it looks fine, you could move on. Others may disagree, but this is now a general SEM question, not a lavaan question.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Hello Pat,

thank you for your time and help.

The factors I standardized are all 2nd order latent factors, and I thought I needed to do it, for the model to be identified - even if the 1st order factors, which are the actual growth curves, all have fixed loadings. Is that not correct?

This all started with a model with 13 parallel processes, which strangely enough did not show any odd results (I deleted 3 of them for theoretical reasons), but I will take your advice, scale it down further and see what insights I can gain.

Federica

Il giorno martedì 28 luglio 2020 alle 14:00:35 UTC+2 mal...@malonequantitative.com ha scritto:
> It's hard to tell all of what's going on here, but you almost certainly don't want to "standardize" all of the latent growth terms.
>
> Since the Is and Ss have their loadings defined, what you've done in the "lv as scaling" section is constrain the variances of all of your latent intercepts to equality over variables and constrain all of the slopes to zero growth/flat over time.
>
> I suggest you try building up from a smaller model until you've got something that works before going to all 10 (!) parallel processes.
>
> Pat
>

At the time, using a "marker variable approach" for the lower-order factors solved the issue, but I don't think I can do it in a bifactor model...
> >
> > I will put my code and results below. Sorry for just dumping it all here like this, but I am truly at a loss and I do not know what information may or may not be relevant. I'll be happy to answer any question or provide more information

messages.body_plain:
Oh, I see.

This is indeed a massive model to start off with.

Another place to look is here:

# Intercepts

IG =~ NA*Imatreas + Iblkdes + Ispantot + Ivpatotal + Ilmtotal + Idigback + Isymsear + Idigsym + Iittotal + Icrtmean

Ivis =~ NA*Imatreas + Iblkdes + Ispantot

Imem =~ NA*Ivpatotal + Ilmtotal + Idigback

Ispeed =~ NA*Isymsear + Idigsym + Iittotal + Icrtmean

# Slopes

SG =~ NA*Smatreas + Sblkdes + Sspantot + Svpatotal + Slmtotal + Sdigback + Ssymsear + Sdigsym + Sittotal + Scrtmean

Svis =~ NA*Smatreas + Sblkdes + Sspantot

Smem =~ NA*Svpatotal + Slmtotal + Sdigback

Sspeed =~ NA*Ssymsear + Sdigsym + Sittotal + Scrtmean

I'm not 100% sure what the NAs do here. Try just SG =~ *Smatreas + Sblldes , etc.

You probably also want to replace

# covariances

IG ~~ SG

Ivis ~~ Svis

Imem ~~ Smem

Ispeed ~~ Sspeed

*******

with

IG ~~ SG

Ivis + Imem + Ispeed + Svis + Smem + Sspeed ~~ Ivis + Imem + Ispeed + Svis + Smem + Sspeed

> For future reference, it would also be helpful to show us the results of cfa(), not just summary(). What did the top of summary() show you, specifically the fit measures?
>
> But here it's easy--your model is unidentified. In most circumstances in a CFA, you need at least three indicators per factor unless you have additional constraints to compensate. SAR and PER each have only two. There's not enough information in the original variance/covariance matrix to estimate this model.
>
> That said, if, as I'd guess, SAR1 and SAR2 are theoretically interchangeable, and likewise for PER1 and PER2, it's probably defensible to do this:
>
> SAR =~ 1*SAR1 + 1*SAR2
> PER =~ 1*PER1 + 1*PER2
>
> With the rest the same. this constrains the two loadings on each first-order factor to be equal, which is a possible "additional constraint" I mentioned.

Andy

messages.subject: Re: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statement?
messages.subject_clean: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statement?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks again for your reply, Yves.

Adding "w WITH x2" to the between model in the Mplus code you provided lines up most everything nicely.  Parameter estimates and just about dead on and number of estimated parameters is equal across the two models.  TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR are a tad off, TLI being really off, but I'm not sure why.  Will continue to investigate but I'm pleased that I know what both Mplus and lavaan are doing in those cases.  Makes sense that a term included on the within but not between level should be detected that way by lavaan--not sure why Mplus insists on identifying such variables, unless it's a useful redundancy for the user.

Best,

Joe

On Tuesday, July 28, 2020 at 2:28:15 AM UTC-6 yros...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hello Joseph,
>
> > What I find interesting is that the observed covariance matrices do not
> > have the same structure at the different levels (which seems an obvious
> > point): within has x1, x2, and y, and between has w, x2, and y.  Mplus,
> > however, includes w at the within level and x1 at the between (with zero
> > variance and covariance for each).
>
> That is just a matter of presentation. Internally, lavaan is using the
> same matrices as Mplus. But only when we need to combine the two levels
> (for computing the loglikelihood) do we 'extend' the matrices to contain
> all within+between variables.
>
> > For the most part, the parameter estimates are the same or close, but
> > the number of estimated free parameters isn't the same.
>
> I believe the difference is due to this Mplus warning:
>
> *** WARNING in MODEL command
> In the MODEL command, the following variable is an x-variable on the
> BETWEEN
> level and a y-variable on the WITHIN level. This variable will be
> treated
> as a y-variable on both levels: X2
>
> lavaan is not doing this (yet?). This is indeed a difference. However,
> my impression is that Mplus is in fact always using 'fixed.x = FALSE'
> when estimating the parameters, but then selectively hides 'exogenous'
> fixed.x parameters from the output by default. If you mention them
> explicitly in the model specification, the number of free parameter
> changes, but the output remains identical:
>
> MODEL:
> %WITHIN%
> y ON x2;
> x2 ON x1;
> x1;
> %BETWEEN%
> y ON x2 w;
> w;
>
> So to get output closer to that of Mplus (in terms of parameter
> estimates), you can use
>
> fit <- sem(mp9.3.l, data=mp9.3.dat, cluster="clus", fixed.x = FALSE)
>
> The default (in lavaan) is fixed.x = TRUE, and in this case (unlike
> Mplus) the exogenous means/variances/covariances are truly fixed to
> their sample values. This often leads to small but noticeable differences.
>
> Yves.

messages.subject: Predict dependent/endogenous variables from new dataset using lavaan path model
messages.subject_clean: Predict dependent/endogenous variables from new dataset using lavaan path model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have constructed a path model with lavaan (regressions only, no latent variables) using a complete dataset (data1) with values for all variables (x's and y's). The R code I used is as follows:
# Specification
model1 <- 'y1 ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + y2
y2 ~ x1 + x2 + x4 + x5 + x6'
# Fit
fit1 <- sem(model = model1, data = data1, estimator = "MLR")

I now want to predict/estimate values for y1 and y2 using a new dataset (data2) which includes values for all x variables, but not for the y variables. In other words, I want to predict unknown values for the y variables using the known x variable values and my fitted path model estimates, similar to prediction in regular regression.

However, from my searches in this Google Group and elsewhere, the lavPredict() function is NOT built to do this (the CRAN description for lavPredict() explicitly states: "the goal of this function is NOT to predict future values of dependent variables as in the regression framework!"; also, here <https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/44>). My understanding is that the regular predict() function will also call lavPredict() for lavaan objects. Though it seems like there were plans to update lavPredict() to be able to conduct regression-style predictions (see here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/LPxosJ7lVpU>), I cannot find any documentation of these suggested updates being implemented.

Is there any way to predict (in a regression sense) values for my dependent variables given values of my independent variables from a new dataset using my lavaan path model (as described above)?

Apologies in advance if I somehow missed the answer to this question elsewhere. Thank you so much!

messages.subject: Re: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statement?
messages.subject_clean: lavaan command comparable to Mplus "within" statement?
messages.body_plain:
On 7/28/20 6:32 PM, Joseph Bonito wrote:
> know what both Mplus and lavaan are doing in those cases.

Actually, after reflecting on this for a while, I do believe that Mplus
(and not lavaan) is doing the "right thing" in this example. Or at least
almost. If 'x2' occurs at both levels, it should indeed be treated as
'endogenous' implying that we should freely estimate its
variance/intercept at the second level.

Currently, by default, lavaan treats is as 'fixed', because it is
exogenous at level-2. But this fixes the variance/intercept at its
sample estimate: the value you see in lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"). This
is suboptimal. I will change this in dev lavaan.

However, 'x2' is still exogenous (at level-2), and therefore, the
covariance between x2 and w should not be fixed to zero. Which is what
Mplus is now implicitly doing! I will make sure these covariances remain
non-zero.

Thanks for providing this interesting example. I had not considered this
setting before.

Yves.

Hi Yves,

You are welcome.  To keep a long story short, I came across it while estimating a model in which two within predictors had the same means at the group level, which is a problem.  The solution was to use only one of the two predictors at the within level while treating the other at as a within-only variable.  Mplus, as we discussed, requires one to do that, which got me wondering how to make lavaan correspond to the Mplus model.  Not that Mplus and its underlying assumptions should be considered the best approach--it shouldn't.  Good to know what's happening under the hood.

Best,

Joe

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

In my path analysis, I'm estimating a parameter "Abs.PM" which takes the ratio of the absolute values of other path coefficients. After fitting the model, I find that the standard error of this Abs.PM parameter is 0, so the Z score and p-value are listed as "NA".
However, if I chose standardized estimates, then the standard error appears just fine.
My questions are: (1) do you know why the raw output is not returning a standard error value for Abs.PM? and (2) Is it possible for me to obtain the SE of the raw output for Abs.PM?

Thank you for your time,
Rak

Code
library(lavaan) #v0.6-5
###:::::: Population Model ::::::###
set.seed(777)
X <- rnorm(200)

messages.subject: Re: error in growth models with multiple imputed data
messages.subject_clean: error in growth models with multiple imputed data
messages.body_plain:
> I get this error (
> Error in D3.LRT(object, h1 = h1, useImps = useImps, asymptotic = asymptotic, : D3 test statistic could not be calculated. Try the D2 pooling method.),
> which I am not sure what it means, or how to fix it.

It means the default D3 test statistic could not be calculated (not sure why), and you can fix it by setting test="D2" when you call lavTestLRT.mi() or anova() (see the ?lavTestLRT.mi help page).

> Do I need to worry about that? Would this be considered a Heywood case as well?

Any negative variance is a Heywood case.  If your model fits poorly, that could be an explanation.  If not, sampling error is another (in my experience, much more commonly) plausible explanation.  You can test the H0 that the variance is truly nonnegative by inspecting whether the 95% CIs include positive values, in which case it is consistent with sampling variability.

https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0049124112442138

> I don't quite understand why to models that are perfectly fitted when analyzed individually

Do you mean the chi-squared = 0?

> lead to a bad fit when combined into a parallel model

Not sure what this means.  Are you referring to a pooled chi-squared, or are you comparing different modeling approaches?

> Negative pooled test statistic was set to zero, so fit will appear to be arbitrarily perfect.
>
> Why is that?

That can happen due to sampling error, especially when the model fits well.  The D3 statistic involves complicated calculations, including fitting the model with parameter estimates fixed at pooled values to each imputation.  If I recall correctly, the D3 pooled stat can be negative when the fixed-model fit is better on average across imputations than the average LRT stat across imputations... something like that.

messages.body_plain:
> (1) do you know why the raw output is not returning a standard error value for Abs.PM?

No, but I don't think percentage-mediated is a meaningful metric when the direct and indirect effects are opposite-signed.  If you do want PM anyway, then at least you need to calculated it as Abs.PM := abs(ab)/abs(ab + direct), because the total effect is the sum of direct and indirect effects, not their absolute values.

> (2) Is it possible for me to obtain the SE of the raw output for Abs.PM?

You could ask for more precision with summary(fit, nd = 6), and you can also find it in the parameterEstimates() output, which is a data.frame, so you could request

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit)
PE$se[PE$lhs == "Abs.PM"]

That's what you asked for. The first indProd line says DataD.dmc <http://DataD.dmc> <- indProd(DataD,...)
This stores the product indicators in the DataD.dmc <http://DataD.dmc> object.
In the second and all following lines you write: DataD.dmc <http://DataD.dmc> <- indProd(DataD,... )

DataD.dmc <http://DataD.dmc> <- indProd(DataD.dmc <http://DataD.dmc>, ...)
